nuggets.body: CrossFit lives in the glycolytic zone — repeated near-max efforts that chew through muscle glycogen (your stored training fuel) fast, so a second session or a long metcon feels flat once the tank runs low. On heavy-volume days aim for roughly 5–7g of carbs per kg of body weight across the day to keep those stores topped up. Eat a carb-focused meal two to three hours before your main WOD.

nuggets.title: Under-fuelling steals your skills
nuggets.body: Gymnastics rewards a lean, powerful frame, but grinding through three-plus hours of repeated explosive attempts on too little energy blunts skill, strength and bone health over time. Protect lean mass and bone by eating enough across the day and hitting roughly 1.6–2.2g of protein per kg of body weight. Never train a long skills session fasted — have a carb-and-protein meal beforehand.

nuggets.title: Graze between burns on a long crag day
nuggets.body: Climbing is stop-start — a hard burn, then a long rest, repeated for hours, with forearms and focus fading as glycogen drains. On long sessions, drip-feed 30–60g of easily-digested carbs per hour so you're not running on empty by your project attempt. Pack simple snacks you can nibble between climbs rather than one heavy meal that sits in your stomach.

nuggets.title: Don't go into an evening class empty
nuggets.body: A 45–60 minute spin, HIIT or bootcamp class is high-intensity from the first minute, so rolling in after a long day with nothing in the tank means light-headedness and a weaker effort. A small snack of 15–30g of carbs, 30–60 minutes before, tops you up without sitting heavy. Grab a banana or a slice of toast before you head in.

nuggets.title: Fuel the working sets, then feed the repair
nuggets.body: Resistance training runs on muscle glycogen for your hard sets, then needs protein to turn that work into muscle. Bookend your session: some carbs beforehand for quality sets, then 20–40g of protein within a few hours afterwards to drive repair. Don't lift fasted and then skip the post-session meal if you want the work to actually count.

nuggets.title: Swimming's hidden hunger
nuggets.body: Hard pool sets burn through muscle glycogen — your stored carbs — quickly, but cold water can mask the hunger until you're suddenly ravenous afterwards. For any swim beyond about 90 minutes, sip a carb drink poolside between sets rather than waiting until you're home to refuel. Keep a bottle on the wall for your next long session.

nuggets.title: Don't ride yourself into the bonk
nuggets.body: Running your glycogen — your muscles' stored carbs — dry mid-ride is 'the bonk', and it ends a good day fast. On rides longer than about two hours, take in roughly 60g of carbs an hour from a mix of bananas, gels and sports drink, and start before you feel empty. Pack that fuel before your next long ride.

nuggets.title: Fuel the long run, gut included
nuggets.body: On runs beyond about 90 minutes your carb stores run low, so aim for around 30-60g of carbs an hour from gels, chews or drink. Just as important, practise it in training — your gut has to be taught to absorb fuel while you pound the road. Trial your race fuel on your next long run, not on race day.

nuggets.title: Bank your fuel on the bike
nuggets.body: You can barely eat mid-swim and a jostling stomach makes running miserable, so the bike is your real feeding window in a long-course race. Take most of your carbs there — around 60g an hour — to top up glycogen before you run off the bike. Rehearse eating on the bike in training so race day feels routine.

nuggets.title: Regatta day is all-day fuelling
nuggets.body: A regatta can mean several races spread across hours, each a brutal effort that empties your carb stores. In the 30-60 minutes between heats, take on easy carbs — around 1g per kg of body weight — plus fluid, rather than sitting on an empty tank. Pack grazing food and drink for your next race day.

nuggets.title: Four quarters, no snack bar in the pool
nuggets.body: Water polo blends sprint swimming, treading water and contact across four quarters — a high, stop-start burn on your carb stores with no chance to eat once you're in. Fuel up beforehand and use the breaks between quarters for a few sips of a carb-electrolyte drink. Stash a bottle on the bench for your next match.

nuggets.title: Cold hides your thirst on the mountain
nuggets.body: A full day on the piste mixes short, hard runs with cold air that dulls your sense of thirst and burns extra energy just keeping you warm. Sip fluids and take on some carbs every hour or two even when you don't feel like it — aim for a drink roughly every hour rather than waiting for the top. Pack easy snacks so a long day never ends on empty.

nuggets.title: Fuel for the third-period sprint
nuggets.body: Hockey is played in short, all-out shifts, so your legs lean on stored carbohydrate (glycogen) that runs low by the third period. Go into a game well-fuelled with a carb-rich meal two to four hours before, then sip a carb drink or nibble something quick each intermission. Topping up between periods keeps your last shifts as sharp as your first.

nuggets.title: Don't let the back nine cost you
nuggets.body: A round is four to five hours of walking and concentration, and a dip in blood sugar late on shows up as sloppy decisions, not just tired legs. Eat a steady snack every five or six holes and keep drinking so your focus on the back nine matches the front. Slow-release foods like a banana, nuts or an oat bar beat one big sugary hit.

nuggets.title: Steady hands start with steady fuel
nuggets.body: Archery asks for fine control and long focus across a tournament day, and big swings in blood sugar or too much caffeine can add the small tremor that misses the gold. Caffeine won't steady your hands — if anything a strong dose can set them shaking — so graze on slow-release snacks between ends and keep coffee to a minimum before you shoot. Bring your own food so an all-day shoot never leaves you light-headed.

nuggets.title: Refuel between the chukkas
nuggets.body: A polo match is several hard riding periods (chukkas) of around seven minutes each, with sprinting and heat draining you across the game. Use the breaks to drink and take on a little carbohydrate so your last chukka has the same snap as your first. In hot weather aim for a good drink each break rather than one big bottle at the end.

nuggets.title: When a walk needs more than water
nuggets.body: For most walks under an hour or so, water is all you need — your body runs happily on stored fuel at that steady pace. Once you're past about ninety minutes, add a light carbohydrate snack and keep drinking to hold your energy and enjoy the miles. Longer or hillier routes are where a small snack in your pocket makes the difference.

nuggets.title: Padel's real test is the second hour
nuggets.body: Social padel rarely stops at one match — an Americano or a long doubles session can keep you on court for two hours or more. That steadily drains glycogen (your muscles' stored carbohydrate), so once a session runs past 90 minutes aim for 30-60g of carbs an hour — a banana and a sports drink between matches covers it. Keep a bottle courtside and sip between games rather than waiting until you fade.

nuggets.title: Badminton burns hotter than it looks
nuggets.body: Those short rallies hide a big workload — constant lunges, jumps and direction changes in a warm indoor hall mean you can lose well over a litre of sweat in a hard singles match. Losing even 2% of your body weight in fluid blunts your footwork and reactions. Drink to thirst through the match and add electrolytes on sweaty days.

nuggets.title: Squash needs fuel in the tank
nuggets.body: Few sports run your engine as hard — a hot, enclosed court and near-continuous rallies can burn well over 600 calories an hour and empty your glycogen (stored carbohydrate) fast. Go in topped up with a carb-rich meal 2-3 hours before, and take a few sips of a sports drink between games in a long best-of-five. Don't start a match already under-fuelled.

nuggets.title: Use the changeover to fuel
nuggets.body: A close match can run past two hours in full sun, and the every-other-game changeover is your built-in fuelling window. Taking in around 30-60g of carbs an hour — the classic banana plus a drink — keeps your legs and focus intact into a third set. Start sipping early, not once you're already flagging.

nuggets.title: Steady fuel keeps your reactions sharp
nuggets.body: Table tennis leans on your brain as much as your legs — split-second reactions and focus that has to hold through a full tournament day of back-to-back matches. Your brain runs mainly on blood glucose, so don't go hours without eating between rounds; a light carb snack every couple of hours keeps concentration and reaction time steady. Pack easy snacks in your kit bag before you go.

nuggets.title: Fuel the fourth quarter
nuggets.body: Basketball is stop-start dynamite — repeated sprints and jumps across four quarters drain glycogen (your muscles' stored carbohydrate), and it's often the final quarter where the tank runs dry. Top up with a carb-rich meal a few hours before tip-off and use half-time for a drink and a quick carb hit. Aim to finish the game as fresh as you started it.

nuggets.title: Jump after jump needs carbs
nuggets.body: Every point is another near-maximal jump, and a tournament can stack match on match across a whole day — beach or indoor, that's a heavy glycogen (stored carbohydrate) drain. Eat a carb-rich meal before you start and graze on 30-60g of carbs an hour between matches; on the beach, add extra fluid and a little salt for the heat. Keep fuel and a bottle in your bag all day.

nuggets.title: Fuel the stop-start game
nuggets.body: Netball is all sharp accelerations, hard stops and changes of direction across four quarters — an interval pattern that leans heavily on your muscles' stored carbohydrate. Go in with a carb-rich meal a few hours before, and use the quarter breaks for a few sips of a sports drink in a tight game. Don't skip the pre-match meal on a busy league night.

nuggets.title: Fuel the long innings, not just the walk out
nuggets.body: A day batting in the middle or fielding in the heat can run for hours, and your concentration fades as your glycogen (stored carbohydrate fuel) drops. Take on 30-60g of carbohydrate an hour across the day — a banana, a gel or a sports drink at drinks, lunch and tea. Pack those snacks in your kit bag before you leave for the ground.

nuggets.title: Win the second half at dinner the night before
nuggets.body: That late-game heavy-legged feeling is glycogen running low after 90 minutes of stop-start sprinting. Front-load roughly 6-8g of carbohydrate per kg of body weight in the 24 hours before kick-off, then take a quick carb top-up at half-time. Plan your pre-match rice or pasta the night before, not on the way to the ground.

nuggets.title: Fuel the collisions, then rebuild them
nuggets.body: Every tackle and ruck is micro-damage your body has to repair, on top of 80 minutes of running. Aim for 1.6-2.0g of protein per kg of body weight across the day, with a carb-rich meal beforehand to power the contact. Get a protein-and-carb meal in within a couple of hours of full time.

nuggets.title: Sweat costs you the sprint
nuggets.body: Field hockey is continuous running in a low, crouched posture, and quarters in the sun drain a lot of fluid. Losing just 2% of your body weight in sweat measurably slows your sprint and dulls your decisions. Sip a carb-electrolyte drink at every quarter break rather than waiting for full time.

nuggets.title: Pads, heat and a three-hour clock
nuggets.body: Under a helmet and pads you can lose over a litre of sweat an hour, and the game itself stretches past three hours. Drink to your thirst on the sideline and take regular carbohydrate so late-game plays stay sharp. Weigh yourself before and after a game to learn how much fluid you actually need to replace.

nuggets.title: Steady fuel for a slow-burn game
nuggets.body: A game runs three hours or more of standing and waiting, broken by all-or-nothing sprints, swings and throws that need fresh reactions. Keep your blood sugar steady with a light carbohydrate snack every hour or two in the dugout, and keep sipping fluid. Stock your bag with easy snacks before first pitch.

nuggets.title: Cover the miles on a full tank
nuggets.body: Lacrosse has you running several kilometres of fast breaks and transitions, so you start draining your glycogen stores early. Eat a carb-rich meal 3-4 hours before face-off to top them up, with a small snack closer to the whistle if you're peckish. Sort your pre-game meal ahead of time so you're not playing on empty.

nuggets.title: Indoor, flat-out, half a tank by the break
nuggets.body: Sixty minutes of jumps, throws and sprints in a warm sports hall burns through glycogen fast. A carbohydrate drink at half-time delivering 30-60g helps you hold your speed and spring into the second half. Have that drink mixed and ready on the bench before the game starts.

nuggets.title: Repeated sprints reward a topped-up tank
nuggets.body: Futsal is near-constant maximal sprinting on a hard court, and well-fuelled players fade far less over rolling subs. Eat a carbohydrate-rich snack one to two hours before you play, and sip a sports drink while you're on the bench. Come to court already fuelled rather than hoping to catch up.

nuggets.title: Don't play your evening game on fumes
nuggets.body: Touch is continuous running with no contact, and an after-work fixture often lands hours after your last proper meal. Have a carbohydrate snack 60-90 minutes before kick-off and get some fluid in, so you're not starting flat and dehydrated. Keep a banana or a cereal bar in your bag for the commute to the pitch.

nuggets.title: Tournaments are won between games
nuggets.body: A tournament can mean three to five games of sprinting, jumping and diving in a single day in the sun. Refuel with 30-60g of carbohydrate plus fluid and a little salt in every gap between games, not just at lunch. Pack a cool bag of snacks and drinks the night before so recovery starts the moment you come off.

nuggets.title: Lifting shapes you — it won't 'bulk' you
nuggets.body: Women carry far less testosterone (the main muscle-building hormone) than men — roughly 10–20 times less — so a sensible strength programme with a small calorie surplus builds athletic, toned muscle, not size overnight. Visible muscle takes months of steady lifting, not a few weeks. Start with two or three full-body strength sessions a week and let it build.

nuggets.title: Progressive overload works the same for you
nuggets.body: The way muscle grows — progressive overload, or gradually asking it to do a little more — doesn't change by sex. Add a rep or two to each set first, and once you can hit your target reps with good form, nudge the weight up by a small amount (about 2.5 kg on the big lifts). Log every session so those small, steady gains are easy to see.

nuggets.title: Don't under-eat protein while you build
nuggets.body: Women building muscle or training hard benefit from the same protein as men — around 1.6–2.2 g per kilogram of body weight a day. The most common gap is simply eating too little, so if progress has stalled, check protein first. Spread it across three or four meals, with a protein source at each.

nuggets.title: Fuel a little more before your period
nuggets.body: In the days before your period your body can burn slightly more energy, so eating a little more then — not less — supports your session quality and steady progress. Think of it as fuelling to perform, not slipping up. Add a small extra snack, roughly 100–200 kcal, around your key training days that week.

nuggets.title: Feeling flat? Get your iron checked
nuggets.body: Regular periods plus heavy endurance training can slowly lower iron — the mineral your blood uses to carry oxygen — and low iron saps stamina; some studies find low stores in as many as 1 in 4 women who train endurance. Too much iron is harmful, so never start supplements to fix it on your own. If you're often unusually flat or breathless, book a simple blood test with your GP rather than guessing.

nuggets.title: Carbs fuel your hardest sessions
nuggets.body: Women rely on carbohydrate — your body's fastest fuel — to power high-intensity work just as men do, so under-fuelling key sessions leaves speed and strength on the table. Aim for a carb-rich meal or snack in the few hours beforehand; around 1 g per kilogram of body weight is a sensible starting point. Fuel the session, then refuel afterwards.

nuggets.title: Build muscle and lose fat at once
nuggets.body: If you're new to lifting or returning after a break, body recomposition — gaining muscle while losing a little fat at the same time — is realistic at maintenance calories with enough protein and consistent strength work. It's slower than chasing one goal at a time, so judge it by your gym strength and progress photos, not the scale. Give it at least 8–12 weeks of steady lifting before you weigh up the results.

nuggets.title: Springy legs run cheaper
nuggets.body: Runners get faster in the gym by getting more economical, not bigger. Heavy, low-rep lifting plus a little plyometric hopping trains the calf-Achilles spring and stretch-shortening cycle, so each stride costs less energy — without piling on weight. Strathlon tunes your plan toward running and adds a reactive finisher on top.

nuggets.title: Heavy legs, faster pedals
nuggets.body: The pedal stroke is a one-leg-at-a-time push, so a cyclist's gym time is best spent on heavy squats and hinges plus single-leg work. That builds the force for a sharper sprint and lets you hold a pace more economically — with little change in body weight. Strathlon blends in this emphasis and adds a cycling finisher.

nuggets.title: A little lifting goes a long way
nuggets.body: Three endurance sports leave little time for the gym — and triathlon doesn't need much. A handful of heavy compound lifts a couple of times a week can improve both cycling and running economy without adding body mass, plus a dash of springy plyometrics for the run. Strathlon tunes the plan toward triathlon and adds a sport finisher.

nuggets.title: Guard the swimmer's shoulder
nuggets.body: Shoulder pain is the swimmer's signature complaint, built from thousands of overhead strokes that overload the internal rotators and leave the cuff and scapular muscles behind. Twice-weekly rotator-cuff and scapular work — external rotations, prone T's and Y's, scapular punches — can help hold that balance across a season. Strathlon adds this shoulder-care work to a swim-tuned plan.

nuggets.title: Row from the legs, not the back
nuggets.body: Every stroke is a leg drive through the hips and back, so the lifts that move the boat are heavy squats, hinges and pulls. A well-drilled deadlift does double duty — building stroke power and grooving the braced, neutral-spine hinge that protects a rower's easily-flared lower back. Strathlon tunes the plan toward rowing and adds a finisher.

nuggets.title: Train your knees before the snow
nuggets.body: The knee — and the ACL especially — is skiing's signature injury. A multi-component routine of balance, landing control, leg strength and plyometrics together is linked to roughly halving ACL injuries, and works best done consistently before the season rather than mid-winter. Strathlon tunes a ski plan toward strong, controllable legs with balance and landing work built in.

nuggets.title: Walking's missing half
nuggets.body: Walking is a superb aerobic base but a gentle one, so it does little for muscle, bone or balance. Strength fills exactly those gaps: heavy squats and hinges load bone the miles can't, while single-leg and balance work steadies each stride and guards against falls. Strathlon tunes a plan toward walking and adds calf, hip and balance work.

nuggets.title: Punch with your legs, not your arm
nuggets.body: A hard punch is a whole-body chain: force starts at the floor and travels up through hip and trunk rotation, and the cross tends to hit hardest because it rides rear-leg drive. So train explosive power and rotational medicine-ball throws, not just bench press. Strathlon tunes your plan toward boxing with a rotational, explosive finisher on a strength base.

nuggets.title: No single quality wins a fight
nuggets.body: MMA asks for everything at once — max strength you can express explosively for takedowns and strikes, an iron grip, a resilient neck, and both energy systems. So get strong first, then train that strength to arrive fast. Strathlon blends the emphasis and adds an MMA finisher plus grip, neck and rotational accessory work on your base plan.

nuggets.title: Grip that lasts, a core that holds
nuggets.body: In jiu-jitsu your grip fades across a roll, so grip endurance — long holds and loaded carries — tends to matter more than a one-rep crush. Pair it with isometric core and hip strength, because guard retention and framing are really about not being moved. Strathlon biases your plan toward that grip, pulling and bracing work.

nuggets.title: Get strong for your size
nuggets.body: Wrestling rewards strength-to-weight, not bulk. Heavy hinges and hard pulling build the posterior chain and grip behind every shot and finish, and positional isometrics let you express force while locked up and tired. A deliberately built, resilient neck helps too. Strathlon tunes your plan toward wrestling with grip, neck and posterior-chain accessory work on a strength base.

nuggets.title: Serve speed starts at the floor
nuggets.body: The serve and groundstrokes are ground-up rotational actions, so explosive rotation — medicine-ball throws and cable chops — tends to transfer to racquet-head speed far better than curls ever will. Build it on single-leg strength that brakes as hard as it accelerates. Strathlon adds a rotational finisher and shoulder-care accessory work to your base plan.

nuggets.title: Guard against padel elbow
nuggets.body: The elbow is padel's signature injury — usually wrist-extensor tendinopathy from all the gripping and overhead striking. The best-supported defence tends to be progressive eccentric wrist-extensor loading, plus grip work, a sensible grip size, and not over-playing through pain. Strathlon can layer this forearm and shoulder-care work onto your padel-tuned plan.

nuggets.title: Squash is played on one leg
nuggets.body: Most shots are struck from a lunge, so single-leg strength — split squats, step-ups, single-leg deadlifts — is your most sport-specific work, alongside the ability to decelerate and change direction. And don't skip heavy calf raises: the calf and Achilles top squash's injury list. Strathlon tunes your plan toward squash with single-leg and calf accessory work.

nuggets.title: Springy legs, harder smash
nuggets.body: Badminton is played off one leg — deep lunges, hard stops, jump smashes. Build single-leg strength first, then add jumps (plyometrics) to make that power springy and fast, which tends to lift jump height and smash quality more than heavy lifting alone. Strathlon tilts your plan toward it with single-leg and reactive finishers.

nuggets.title: It's not all in the wrist
nuggets.body: Table tennis looks like a wrist game, but the fast bat comes from the ground up — legs and hips feeding a rotating trunk. Medicine-ball rotational throws build that power, trained as power: few reps, full intent, full recovery, not to fatigue. Strathlon adds a rotational-power finisher to your plan.

nuggets.title: Speed beats stretch
nuggets.body: Clubhead speed tends to track with whole-body power, not flexibility. Build force with squats and hinges, then express it fast with jumps and rotational medicine-ball throws that train the X-factor — the hip-shoulder separation a big backswing turn alone won't give you. Strathlon tilts your plan toward that rotational power.

nuggets.title: A steadier hold is a stronger one
nuggets.body: Archery is stability and endurance, not power. The steadiest shots come from back, rotator-cuff and scapular endurance — plus a strength base that makes the draw feel submaximal, so your muscles tremble less under it. Strathlon leans your plan toward lighter, higher-rep pulling and cuff work.

nuggets.title: Build a bowler-proof trunk
nuggets.body: Cricket's signature demand is fast bowling: the front foot lands under several times body weight. A strong posterior chain and anti-rotation trunk both produce that force and survive it, while rotational power feeds bat and ball speed — and Nordic-style work can help guard the hamstrings. Strathlon adds cricket rotational, single-leg and shoulder-care work.

nuggets.title: Power comes from rotation
nuggets.body: A swing and a throw are the same move — power from the ground up through a fast-rotating trunk. Rotational medicine-ball throws build that sequenced power and tend to track bat and throwing velocity, but only on a base of heavy lower-body strength; protect the throwing arm with cuff and scapular work. Strathlon layers both on.

nuggets.title: Strength per kilo wins
nuggets.body: Gymnastics is a relative-strength sport — force for every kilo you carry. It rewards straight-arm and static (isometric) holding strength and a braced core that ordinary lifting misses, and heavier low-rep work builds strength with little added size, raising power-to-weight so skills feel easier, not harder. Strathlon adds a straight-arm, core and landing layer.

nuggets.title: Fingers first, but progress slowly
nuggets.body: Finger and grip strength is what really limits climbers — but the finger pulleys are also the most-injured tissue, so build finger load up slowly, over weeks not days. Favour open-hand grips, warm up well, and never climb through sharp finger pain. Strathlon tilts your gym plan toward climbing with a grip finisher on a pulling-and-pressing base.

nuggets.title: Power the swing from your core
nuggets.body: The mallet swing is a hip-to-shoulder rotation, so train both halves: build rotational power with medicine-ball throws and cable rotations, then an anti-rotation core (Pallof press, loaded carries) so that power reaches the mallet instead of leaking through a soft trunk. Train both sides, even though you swing one way. Strathlon adds rotational and core accessories to your base plan.

nuggets.title: Win on the lunge
nuggets.body: Fencing is decided by the lunge — you explode off one leg, then brake and recover on the other. So train it with single-leg lifts (split squats, single-leg RDLs) plus jumps for reactive speed, and build eccentric deceleration strength — the front knee absorbs every lunge and is fencing's most-injured spot. Strathlon tilts your plan toward single-leg and explosive fencing work.

nuggets.title: Nordic curls save hamstrings
nuggets.body: Hamstring strains are football's most common injury, and the Nordic hamstring curl is the standout defence — it tends to roughly halve hamstring-injury rates. Build it gradually, pair it with regular sprinting so match speed isn't a shock, and keep doing it; consistency is the active ingredient. Strathlon adds hamstring and single-leg work to your football plan.

nuggets.title: Get strong, then make it fast
nuggets.body: Rugby is won and survived in the collision, so heavy strength — squat, hinge, press and pull — is the base: it makes you harder to move and tends to lower injury risk, not slower. Then turn it into contact speed with jumps, throws and sprints, and don't skip cheap neck work. Strathlon tunes your plan with a rugby finisher and power accessories on that base.

nuggets.title: Build the jump, train the landing
nuggets.body: A bigger vertical comes from two things trained together: heavy squats and hinges for force, then plyometrics — jumps, bounds, pogos — to fire it fast. Just as important, train to land and stop, not only to jump: controlled decelerations and stick landings build the eccentric strength that protects your knees. Strathlon adds a plyometric finisher and single-leg work to your basketball plan.

nuggets.title: It's the landing, not the jump
nuggets.body: Netball is played and landed on one leg, and its ACL and ankle injuries strike on uncontrolled landings and hard stops — not the jump itself. So single-leg strength (split squats, single-leg RDLs), deliberate soft, balanced landings, and a few minutes of balance work are the highest-value training you can do. Strathlon tilts your plan toward single-leg and landing work.

nuggets.title: Throw from the ground up
nuggets.body: Handball's jump throw is a whole-body whip, not an arm action — ball speed comes from the legs and trunk driving the shoulder. Heavy squats and hinges plus rotational medicine-ball throws tend to raise throwing velocity more than arm work alone. Strathlon tunes your plan toward handball with a throwing-power finisher on a strength base.

nuggets.title: Own the low stance
nuggets.body: Field hockey lives in a bent-forward, stick-low crouch, so every sprint and tackle fires from a flexed trunk and hips. A strong posterior chain — heavy hip hinges plus anti-rotation trunk work — tends to power that stance and protect the lower back it loads. Strathlon leans your plan toward hockey with posterior-chain and single-leg accessory work.

nuggets.title: Guard the groin
nuggets.body: Skating is a sideways push, so the adductors both power your stride and take the strain — groin pulls are hockey's signature injury. Dedicated adductor work like the Copenhagen exercise, kept up through the season, can cut that risk while making your stride stronger. Strathlon adds hockey adductor and single-leg accessory work on a strength base.

nuggets.title: Train the landing
nuggets.body: Lacrosse is won on cuts, plants and landings — the exact moments the ACL is most exposed, and women's lacrosse carries one of the highest ACL rates in sport. Neuromuscular work — single-leg strength, balance and controlled landing done consistently — tends to lower that risk. Strathlon layers single-leg and jump-landing work onto your lacrosse plan.

nuggets.title: Power the eggbeater
nuggets.body: Water polo happens from an unstable base — your eggbeater kick builds the platform you shoot and block from. Strong hips and legs, plus hip external-rotation and adductor work, tend to raise you higher in the water and protect the medial knee the kick grinds on. Strathlon tunes your plan toward water polo with leg, hip and shoulder-care work.

nuggets.title: Brake as hard as you sprint
nuggets.body: Futsal packs in nearly as many hard stops as sprints — you re-accelerate in a new direction over and over on a grippy court. Single-leg strength and eccentric work to absorb braking tend to sharpen your cutting and spare the ankles, knees and hamstrings it punishes. Strathlon biases your plan toward futsal with single-leg and explosive accessory work.

nuggets.title: Strong first, then explosive
nuggets.body: A football play is a five-second, all-out collision, so the game rewards raw strength turned into fast power. Heavy squats, hinges and pulls build the force; jumps, throws and short sprints teach you to unleash it — and getting stronger tends to make you faster, not slower. Strathlon tunes your plan toward football with an explosive finisher on a strength base.

nuggets.title: You brake more than you burst
nuggets.body: Touch involves more hard decelerations than accelerations, and you cut and stop on one leg. So bias your gym work toward single-leg strength — split squats, single-leg RDLs — plus Nordic hamstring curls, which tend to make you a sharper cutter and more strain-resistant at once. Strathlon layers these as a touch finisher on a strength base.

nuggets.title: Land soft, cut on a bent knee
nuggets.body: Most ultimate knee and ankle injuries happen with no contact — during your own cutting, pivoting and jump-landings, often on one leg. Neuromuscular work that drills soft, aligned landings and controlled cuts can meaningfully lower ACL risk. Keep it as a short warm-up you actually stick with, year-round.

nuggets.title: The jump is strength plus spring
nuggets.body: No single lift owns your vertical — it's built from two things. Heavy squats and hinges raise the force your legs can produce, and plyometric jump training teaches you to release it fast off the floor. Combining both tends to beat either alone, and rehearsing soft landings guards the knees.

nuggets.title: Get strong, metcons get cheaper
nuggets.body: In CrossFit it's easy to chase conditioning and under-build raw strength — yet a heavier squat, deadlift and press make every rep in a workout a smaller fraction of your max, so the metcon costs you less. Build the strength base first; skill and engine sit on top of it, not instead.

nuggets.title: Classes are your cardio
nuggets.body: Group classes already deliver the conditioning; what they rarely give is progressive, trackable loading — you seldom know exactly what you lifted last week. Adding a couple of structured strength sessions with the weights written down turns 'am I getting stronger?' from a guess into a fact, and tends to protect your shoulders, back and knees too.

nuggets.title: Overload the big patterns
nuggets.body: Gym progress isn't random exercises — it's progressive overload on a few big patterns: squat, hinge, push, pull, carry and core, balanced across the week. Nudge weight or reps up a little over time, and keep your pulling volume matched to your pressing, which tends to keep shoulders healthy. Track it so 'more than last time' is a glance, not a guess.
